fixes.explanation: I get why you'd reach for the elders, friend. They show up in Deuteronomy 25. But in verse 4 Moses doesn't ask for approval. He says the first husband "…may not remarry her…" and he gives the reason: it is "…an abomination to the LORD." No permission slip would change that.

Serving the priests is a fine thing, friend, but it's not what Moses says. He says the newlywed must not be sent to war or be pressed into any duty. For one year he is free "…to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married."

Not quite, friend. Moses never says the millstones belong to the town. His reason is that taking them "…would be taking one’s livelihood as security." The stones are the man's own, and his living is tied up in them.

Yes, Miriam! Moses says, "Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the journey after you came out of Egypt." He brings her up right after the instructions about skin diseases. Miriam was Moses' sister (Numbers 26:59), and her story is told in Numbers 12:10.

Close, friend, since Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), speaks up in that very story (Numbers 12:11). But Moses names someone else in this verse. He says, "Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam…" Her name is the one on the page.

True! Moses says, "…this will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God." That's said about returning the poor man's security by sunset, so that he may sleep in his own cloak. The LORD counts that as righteousness. A cloak handed back is a good return, friend.

Yes. Moses says to pay his wages each day before sunset, "…because he is poor and depends on them." So that pay isn't a small thing to him. Moses warns that if it's held back, the man may cry out to the LORD, and the one holding it back will be guilty of sin (Deuteronomy 24:15).

Not quite, friend. Moses says, "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers…" So a son isn't put to death for his father. The verse ends with "each is to die for his own sin."
Not this one, baker. Moses says, "Fathers shall not be put to death for their children…" So a father isn't put to death for his children. The verse ends with "each is to die for his own sin."

Yes! Moses says, "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place." Then he adds, "Therefore I am commanding you to do this." So the reason he gives is Israel's own story: slaves in Egypt, redeemed by the LORD. That's a whole lot of history packed into one "remember," friend.

Test is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the word in this verse. Moses says the LORD "…may bless you in all the work of your hands." The forgotten sheaf is to be left for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. And that is tied to blessing.

Sunset does come up in Deuteronomy 24, baker, but not here. In verse 3, Moses says the limit is "…lest your brother be beaten any more than that and be degraded in your sight." Nothing about the clock. The reason is the man himself.

A house is a sensible thing to worry about, friend, but the text doesn't mention one here. Moses says the first son "…will carry on the name of the dead brother, so that his name will not be blotted out from Israel." That's the reason he gives, and it's all about the name.

Yes. She says, "My husband’s brother refuses to preserve his brother’s name in Israel. He is not willing to perform the duty of a brother-in-law for me." Moses has her bring this to the elders at the city gate. Her complaint is that he refuses to preserve his brother's name.

Yes. Moses says to keep accurate and honest weights and measures "…so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you." Honest scales and a long life in the land go together in this verse, friend. A bag with one heavy weight and one light weight is exactly what he forbids (Deuteronomy 25:13). A scale that changes its mind depending on the customer is no scale at all.

Fair is a good word, baker, but the tithe isn't what Moses mentions. He says honest weights and measures are for this: "…so that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you." The reason he gives is living long in the land, not what the priests receive.

Yes, fear. Moses says of the Amalekites, "they had no fear of God." He recalls how they met Israel on the journey when the people were tired and weary, and attacked all the stragglers. That's what Moses names about them, baker.
